USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current escalated posture (25% on ~$200B of Chinese goods plus the May 15 Huawei/ICT action) as leverage, but do not execute the threatened ~$300B round that would directly tax U.S. consumers and tech supply chains. Keep the negotiating channel open toward the possible Xi meeting, pressing China to come back to the table without making new unilateral concessions or adding self-harming escalation.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to U.S. interests is material but not existential. The dispute is already biting: the 10-year Treasury yield fell from ~2.51 around May 6 to 2.37 by May 15 (with a partial inversion of 3-month above 10-year noted by the NYT on May 13), and the Dow dropped 617 points on May 13 after China retaliated with tariffs on ~$60B of U.S. goods (timeline, 2019-05-13). The farm belt is the clearest political casualty — soybean prices ran 20-25% below pre-tariff levels and net farm income fell from $75B to $63B, with the American Soybean Association urging the administration on May 13 to "hold off on additional tariffs" and conclude a deal. That is a material GDP/export drag and mounting domestic political pressure, which supports a moderate threat.reading around +0.4 (between the 0.0 neutral and +0.5 high anchors, and well short of the +1.0 supply-chain/tech existential anchor). The action stance is deliberately not escalating further: the ~$300B next round (public hearing June 17) would hit consumer goods such as iPhones and apparel — the AAFA estimated it would cost a family of four ~$500/year — harming U.S. consumers and risking a deeper market selloff, while the U.S. has already secured substantial leverage with the current 25% tariffs and the Huawei action. Given escalating further has rising domestic costs and diminishing returns, the right move is to hold leverage and negotiate rather than concede or pile on more tariffs.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current posture — maintain the retaliatory tariff hikes we already announced on May 13 on the ~$60B list, but do not escalate further (no rare-earths export controls, no broader retaliation) and keep negotiating channels open for a resumption of talks. We should signal firm resolve without deepening a self-harming spiral while the US has already chosen to walk away from the April progress.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is high. In the space of ten days the US unilaterally collapsed the negotiations that were progressing through April (event 2019-04-03), raised List 3 tariffs from 10% to 25% on ~$200B (2019-05-10), threatened the remaining ~$300B of imports, and on May 15 signed EO 13873 and placed Huawei and 70 affiliates on the Entity List — direct firm-level targeting of our tech champion that jeopardizes tech self-sufficiency and 5G ambitions. This sits at the +0.5 'high' CHN anchor and a bit above, given tariffs now hit ~$250B of our exports at an effective 25% rate and the pain is already visible in the real economy: April retail sales growth was the slowest in 16 years (7.2% vs 8.7% in March), industrial output slumped to 5.4% vs 8.5% in March, and fixed-asset investment missed forecasts (Al Jazeera, 2019-05-15); December exports had already fallen 4.4%. I set threat at +0.6 — serious but not existential, because we retain levers (domestic stimulus, a large domestic market, autonomy/nationalist narrative, and the fact that the US is also self-harming). On action, we should neither capitulate nor over-escalate. Conceding now (a +1 concession) would reward Trump's take-it-or-leave-it escalation and embolden further demands; but escalating further after our May 13 retaliation would damage an already-softening economy and hand Washington domestic cover. The disciplined middle is to hold at our announced retaliation, avoid new escalatory steps, and stand ready to return to talks — which warrants action_score ~0.0 and holding. The US move to punish Huawei also gives us domestic political room and negotiating leverage; we should use it to argue China is the defender of open, rules-based trade rather than to over-respond.
